Layout `columns` over a comment whose body is valid UTF-8 followed by a byte that is not: the invalid byte gets a fixed width and no decoding is attempted over it.
Layout `columns` after a removed HTML comment that spans lines: column positions are recomputed from the current line, not from the original offsets.
Bytes that are not UTF-8 around a comment are copied through untouched, and the CRLF ending survives.
Layout `compact` over a comment between two tokens on one line: nothing about the line changes but the comment, so `compact` leaves exactly what `lines` leaves, the separating space included.

Layout `compact` takes a line that held nothing but a removed comment away entirely, its terminator included, so a run of whole-line comments disappears instead of leaving a run of blank lines. Layout `lines` keeps all four lines.
Layout `compact`: only whitespace stood before the comment on its line, so the indentation goes with the line rather than staying behind as trailing whitespace.
Layout `compact` over CRLF endings: the terminator removed with the line is that line's own CRLF, and the lines that survive keep theirs byte for byte.
Layout `compact` trims the whitespace a removal would otherwise leave at the end of a line, on both sides of the comment. Code survives on each line, so each keeps its terminator.
Layout `compact` over a file that ends without a final newline: the trailing comment and the space before it go, and no terminator is invented for the line that survives.
Layout `compact`: the last line held nothing but the comment and had no terminator of its own, so the line goes and the line before it keeps the terminator it always had.

ISO C17 6.4.9p1: `/*` ... `*/` is one comment however many lines it spans. Layout `compact` keeps the code before it on a line of its own, ends that line with the terminator that ended it in the source, and drops the lines that held only comment.
ISO C17 6.4.9p1. Layout `compact`: every line the block comment covered held nothing else, so all of them go, terminators included.

ISO C17 6.4.9p1. Layout `compact` over a block comment that runs to the end of a file with no final newline: the line the code is on kept its terminator inside the comment, so that terminator comes back, and the last line held only comment and goes.
Layout `compact` judges being alone on a line from the original bytes: neither comment was, so the line keeps its terminator, and the trim closes the gap the first removal left before the second.

HTML 13.2.5.4x: `<!--` ... `-->` is one comment token. An HTML comment closes up completely under every layout, the newlines it spanned included; `compact` adds the whole-line rule and the trim, and never takes the terminator of a line where code survives.
ECMA-262 12.3: U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR is a LineTerminator, so it ends a SingleLineComment. Layout `compact` removes it with the line it terminated and leaves the other one alone.
Layout `compact` over a kept directive above a removed comment: a comment that survives is content on its line, so only the line of the removed one goes.

POSIX 2.2.2 single quotes: an unterminated single quote is a lexical error, reported as an error diagnostic that makes the report invalid.
POSIX 2.7.4: a here-document whose delimiter never arrives is a lexical error, reported as an error diagnostic that makes the report invalid.
POSIX 2.6.3: an unterminated `$(` is a lexical error, and the comment inside it is still located.

Rust Reference, Tokens (string literals): a `"` literal carries a bare newline as content, so this one is closed by nothing and the `//` inside it is never a comment. The diagnostic names the construct that was left open -- `unterminated string` -- rather than saying `literal`, and the two implementations must spell the message the same way, because a message is what a user reads. The recorded block pins the code and the span; the byte-for-byte comparison in `tools/differential.py` is what pins the text.

Go specification, String literals: an interpreted string literal may not contain a newline, so this one ends unterminated at the line break. Go spells one diagnostic for both of its quoted forms -- `unterminated string or rune literal` -- because `"` and `'` are the same failure to a reader scanning the line.

CSS Syntax Module Level 3, 4.3.5: consuming a string that reaches the end of input is a parse error. The diagnostic names the language as well as the construct -- `unterminated CSS string` -- because a CSS string is also what an HTML `<style>` element hands this scanner.
CSS Syntax Module Level 3, 4.3.5: `'` and `"` open the same token, so an unclosed one carries the same `unterminated CSS string` message whichever quote wrote it.

JSON5 4.4 and RFC 8259 7: a string ends at its closing quote, and a newline is not one, so this key is never closed. The diagnostic names the construct as JSON sees it -- `unterminated JSON string` -- for both of the quotes JSON5 allows.

Kotlin language specification, Character literals: a character literal is one character between apostrophes and may not span a line. The diagnostic names it `unterminated Kotlin character literal`, which is what tells it from the `unterminated Kotlin string` a `"` literal reports.

Rust Reference, Tokens (Lifetimes and loop labels): `'` followed by an identifier and *not* closed by a second `'` is a lifetime, not the opening of a character literal. It therefore opens nothing, and the line comment that follows on the same line is an ordinary comment rather than string content.

Rust Reference, Tokens: a character literal holds exactly one character before its closing `'`, so `'` followed by `/` and then another `/` cannot be one. The apostrophe lexes as a lifetime opener and consumes nothing, which leaves the `//` after it opening a line comment -- the reading that removes a comment rather than the one that hides the rest of the file inside a literal.

Rust Reference, Tokens (character literals): a character literal holds one character and ends at the line, so this one is never closed -- the `\` in front of the second apostrophe carries it into the literal as an escape, and no third one arrives before the line break. It is also the shape that tells a literal from a lifetime -- a non-ASCII character with an apostrophe close enough behind it to be the closing quote -- which is why the diagnostic here is `unterminated character literal` and `parity-rust-lifetime-is-not-a-literal` reports nothing at all. Both apostrophes stand on one line because that lookahead stops at a line terminator (`rust-char-literal-across-newline`). Ground truth, `rustc` 1.97: `error[E0762]: unterminated character literal` for this line.

JSON5 specification, 4.4 (Strings): a JSON5 string may be written with apostrophes, and this repository's `jsonc` language is documented as `JSON with comments, including JSON5` and claims the `.json5` extension. So `'` opens a string here exactly as `"` does, and a `//` inside one is content.

JSON5 specification, 4.4: a single-quoted string ends at its closing apostrophe, and a newline is not one. The failure is the same one a `"` string reports, under the same `unterminated JSON string` message.

Rust Reference, Tokens (raw string literals): `r"` ends only at the matching `"` and takes no escapes, so a raw string with no closing quote runs to the end of the file and is an error. The diagnostic spans the literal from its `r` to the end of the source, which is the extent the lexer consumed.

cases.source_utf8: let s = r#"unclosed // not a comment
cases.note: Rust Reference, Tokens: a hashed raw string closes at `"#` for the same number of hashes it opened with. Without that closer the literal reaches the end of the file, the `//` inside it is content rather than a comment, and the source is reported invalid.

Layout `compact` drops a line that held nothing but a removed comment. What counts as nothing is ASCII whitespace as `u8::is_ascii_whitespace` defines it -- space, tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return -- and the vertical tab (U+000B) is deliberately not in that set, the same set Lua's own `isspace` is documented to differ from in `lua_is_space`. So the line here is not blank, the vertical tab survives the removal, and only the comment goes.

The same layout rule as `parity-vertical-tab-python`, in a language whose comment opener is two bytes: a vertical tab before the comment is content, not blank, so `compact` cannot swallow the line it sits on.

The same layout rule again in Lua, where the vertical tab *is* whitespace to the language's own lexer (`lua_is_space`) and still is not whitespace to the layout arithmetic. The two are different questions: one asks what the chunk means, the other asks what the file looks like.

`classify_comment` trims the comment body before it looks for a directive word, and it trims Unicode whitespace -- every scalar with the White_Space property, which U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR has -- and not only the ASCII five. A line separator in front of `region` therefore still leaves the folding-region directive an editor reads, and `safe` keeps it. Keeping is also the conservative half of the disagreement: the alternative deletes a directive because of an invisible character.
The same trim in a `#` comment: U+2028 is whitespace to the classifier, so the `region` behind it is still the directive.
U+00A0 NO-BREAK SPACE also carries White_Space, and it is the one a word processor is most likely to have put there, so a `region` marker written with one is still a directive.
The same rule for a block comment, where the trim has to run past the closing marker `strip_comment_markers` removed as well as the opening one.

POSIX Shell Command Language, 2.3 Token Recognition: `#` opens a comment only where a word does not already begin. A UTF-8 BOM is ordinary word bytes to a shell -- `bash` reads `\ufeff#!/bin/sh` as a command name and reports it not found -- and `execve` requires `#!` at byte 0 as well, so a BOM in front of a shebang line leaves neither a comment nor a preamble. Nothing is removed because nothing was found.

CPython `tokenizer.c`, `check_bom`: a UTF-8 BOM is consumed before the first line is read, so the `#!` line is still the first line of the program. The shebang rule in `classify_comment` skips the same three bytes, reads a shebang, and `safe` keeps it -- the same three bytes `is_python_encoding_declaration` already skips when it looks for a `coding:` line.

Lua 5.4 `lauxlib.c`: `skipcomment` calls `skipBOM` before it tests the first byte for `#`, so a BOM in front of a `#!` line still leaves the loader skipping that whole line. The scanner skips the same three bytes before it applies the first-line rule, and the line is then a kept shebang.

Lua 5.4 `lauxlib.c`, `skipcomment`: the byte the loader looks for after the BOM is `#`, not `#!`, so any first line opening with it is skipped. Without the second byte it is no preamble, only a line comment, and `safe` removes it -- the BOM-carrying twin of `lua-hash-first-line`.

Taplo reads `#:schema` as the directive naming the JSON schema the file is validated against. The keyword ends at a boundary so that prose running letters on past it is not mistaken for the directive, and the end of the comment is such a boundary: `#:schema` with its URL still to be typed is the directive it is about to be, and protecting it costs one line that a formatter would have rewritten anyway. The same reading protects a bare `# shellcheck` and a bare `# hadolint`.

The other half of the boundary: letters running on past `:schema` are prose about schemas rather than Taplo's directive, so this comment is removed. Protecting the bare keyword above must not protect this.

ShellCheck answers to its own name and takes its argument after whitespace, so the keyword ends at a boundary. A directive whose argument is missing is still the directive -- the same end-of-comment boundary `toml-schema-directive-without-argument` records -- while `# shellcheckish note` stays prose.

C++ [lex.string] with [lex.token]: `R"` opens a raw string literal only where it opens a token. Letters running into it do not -- maximal munch reads `aR` as an identifier and `"(x)"` as an ordinary string literal -- so the raw string rules do not apply and the trailing line comment is a comment. The boundary is the same one `parity-rust-unterminated-raw-string` needs for Rust's `r"`.

C++ [lex.string]: a d-char is any member of the basic source character set except space, `(`, `)`, `\`, and the control characters horizontal tab, vertical tab, form feed and new-line. A vertical tab in the delimiter therefore makes this no raw string at all: the `"` opens an ordinary literal, which a newline leaves unterminated. Asking `is_ascii_whitespace` instead would read the raw string, because that predicate leaves the vertical tab out.

ECMA-262 12.2: <VT> U+000B is `WhiteSpace`. So the `<` after it is still preceded by an identifier, which makes it the relational operator and not the opening of a JSX element; the line comment at the end is then an ordinary comment. `u8::is_ascii_whitespace` leaves the vertical tab out, which is why this rule is asked of a predicate of its own.
The same ECMA-262 12.2 rule under the `tsx` dialect, where a mis-read `<` would start a JSX element and swallow the rest of the file.

ECMA-262 B.1.3: the single-line HTML-like close comment `-->` opens a comment only where nothing but whitespace precedes it on the line. <VT> is whitespace there for the same reason it is everywhere else in the grammar, so this `-->` opens a comment.

OCaml manual, 11.1 (Lexical conventions): a character literal is one character between apostrophes, and an escape is one character -- `\\` names a backslash and `\'` an apostrophe. These bytes name two, and the second escape carries off the apostrophe that would have closed the literal, so nothing closes it before the line ends. `ocamlc` 5.5.0 answers the line with `Illegal backslash escape in string or character`. The rest of the file is still a file: the scan resumes where the literal stopped and finds the block comment on the next line, rather than treating one bad literal as the end of what can be read. Both apostrophes stand on one line because the lookahead that finds the second stops at a line terminator (`ocaml-char-literal-across-newline`).

POSIX Shell Command Language, 2.3: `#` opens a comment only where the current character is not part of a word. <blank> is space and tab, and a vertical tab is neither, so it begins a word and the `#` behind it is an ordinary word character. Nothing is a comment and nothing is removed.

The same rule for a byte that is not whitespace at all. A NUL is an ordinary word character to the token recogniser, so it opens a word and the `#` behind it opens no comment. Reading every byte below space as a blank -- which is the tempting shortcut -- would delete this line.

POSIX Shell Command Language, 2.7.4: the here-document delimiter is a word, and a word ends at an unquoted operator character. `>` is one, so this is a here-document named `EOF` and a redirection to `out`, not a here-document named `EOF>out` that would swallow the rest of the file and leave the comment unfound.

HTML Standard, 13.2.5.8 (Tag name state): a tag name ends at ASCII whitespace -- tab, line feed, form feed, carriage return, space -- or at `/` or `>`. A vertical tab is none of those, so this element is named `script\u{b}` and is not the raw-text `script` element; the `//` inside it is text rather than an embedded JavaScript comment.

A declarative profile's `requires_boundary` asks that the delimiter open a token rather than continue one, and the byte before it decides. The question is the engine's own rather than any language's, and the engine's answer is ASCII whitespace: a vertical tab is not a boundary and a line feed is, so the first `REM` here is not a comment and the second is.

ECMA-262 12.5: a hashbang comment opens a Script or a Module and nothing else, and OComment reads that as `a file`: a preamble is a preamble at absolute offset 0. The content of a `<script>` element begins after the tag that opened it, so the `#!` here is not the page's preamble -- no page has one -- and no comment is found inside the element at all. The HTML comment on the next line is still found, and `safe` keeps it, which is what says the scan of the element did not swallow the rest of the file.

cases.note: Ruby 3.3 literals.rdoc and parse.y `parse_slash`: a `/` after a bare word, with white space in front of it and none behind it, opens a regular expression that the word takes as a command argument. Ruby tells a method name from a local variable by the symbol table its parser is building, and a scanner has none, so every bare word is read as a command here: the second line is a pattern to this scanner where Ruby, knowing `a` to be a variable, reads two divisions. That approximation only ever keeps more bytes inside a literal, so it loses a comment rather than inventing one.

Zig Language Reference, Doc comments: `///` documents the declaration under it and `//!` the container the file is, and both are documentation comments. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: `container_doc_comment "//! module"` at [0,10), `doc_comment "/// doc"` at [24,31), and no token for the `// line` comment, which is how the tokenizer reports an ordinary one. `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

Zig Language Reference, Doc comments: exactly three slashes document anything, and a fourth takes the marker back — `.doc_comment_start` falls to `.line_comment` when it meets one. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: no token at all for `//// divider`, `doc_comment "/// doc"` at [13,20). `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

cases.source_utf8: const a = 1 /* not a comment */ + 2; // remove
cases.note: Zig Language Reference, Comments: Zig has one comment form and it is `//`. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: `/*` is `slash` then `asterisk` and `*/` is `asterisk` then `slash`, seven ordinary tokens between the two operands and no comment, so only the `//` behind them is removed. (`zig ast-check` refuses this line for a reason of its own — a binary operator with white space on one side only — and the tokenizer is what decides whether a comment is there.)

Zig Language Reference, String Literals: consecutive `\\` lines are one multiline string literal, and each is its own token that ends before its newline, so the line under them starts in code again. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: `multiline_string_literal_line` at [14,19) and [24,29), then `semicolon` at [30,31). `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

Zig Language Reference, String Literals: everything from a `\\` to the end of its line is string content, and the tokenizer takes that opener wherever a token may begin rather than only as the first thing on a line. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: `multiline_string_literal_line` at [14,34) and at [47,65), so both `//` runs are content and only the last line is a comment. `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

Zig Language Reference, Primitive Values and String Literals: a character literal takes the same backslash escapes a string does, so `'\''` is one literal and the `"` inside one opens nothing. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: `char_literal` at [10,14), [26,37) and [49,52). `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

Zig Language Reference, Identifiers: `@"..."` names an identifier that is not a legal bare name, and the tokenizer lexes it through its string-literal state, so a `//` written inside one is part of the name. Ground truth, `std.zig.Tokenizer` 0.16.0: `identifier "@\"id // x\""` at [6,16) and `identifier "@\"if\""` at [28,33). `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

Zig standard library, `std/zig/Ast/Render.zig`: the formatter takes `"//".len` bytes off the trimmed comment, trims the white space behind them, and compares the remainder with `zig fmt: off` and `zig fmt: on` for equality — so the first two lines are instructions a removal keeps and the third, which merely opens with the phrase, is an ordinary comment. `zig ast-check` accepts the file.

R's own parser draws no such distinction: Ground truth, R 4.3.3 `utils::getParseData(parse(file =, keep.source = TRUE))` gives all four lines the same `COMMENT` token, at [0,8), [9,28), [29,39) and [60,70).

Ground truth, R 4.3.3 `utils::getParseData(parse(file =, keep.source = TRUE))`: `STR_CONST` at [5,33) spanning three lines, with the only `COMMENT` at [34,42).

Ground truth, R 4.3.3 `utils::getParseData(parse(file =, keep.source = TRUE))`: four `STR_CONST` tokens at [5,19), [25,39), [45,59) and [65,80), with the only `COMMENT` at [88,96).

cases.source_utf8:
a <- r"--(dashes ) # x)--"
b <- r"---[deep ]-- # x]---"
c <- 1 # remove
cases.note: `?Quotes`: any number of dashes may stand between the quote and the opening bracket, and the literal closes only on the matching bracket with the same run of dashes and the same quote — which is what lets the closing bracket itself appear as content. R puts no limit on the run: 100 dashes were measured accepted on R 4.3.3. Ground truth, R 4.3.3 `utils::getParseData(parse(file =, keep.source = TRUE))`: `STR_CONST` at [5,26) and [32,55), with the only `COMMENT` at [63,71).

`?Quotes`: the closing run of dashes must be as long as the opening one, so a raw string one dash short never closes and swallows the rest of the file. Ground truth, R 4.3.3: the file is refused with `unexpected INCOMPLETE_STRING`, and the transformation writes nothing.

R Language Definition, 10.3.2: a name may be written between backquotes, and anything at all may go inside — a `#` included. Ground truth, R 4.3.3 `utils::getParseData(parse(file =, keep.source = TRUE))`: `SYMBOL` `` `odd # name` `` at [0,12), with the only `COMMENT` at [18,26).

A backquoted name is lexed like a string and carries a line break as content, so one that never closes runs to the end of the file. Ground truth, R 4.3.3: refused with `unexpected INCOMPLETE_STRING` at column 1 of line 1.

x <- 1 %a # b% 2 # remove
y <- 3 %in% c(1, 2) # also
cases.note: R 4.3.3 `gram.y`, `SpecialValue`: a `%` runs to the next `%` on the same line and every byte between them is part of the operator's name, so a `#` written inside one is not a comment. Ground truth, R 4.3.3 `utils::getParseData(parse(file =, keep.source = TRUE))`: `SPECIAL` `%a # b%` at [7,14) and `%in%` at [33,37), with `COMMENT` at [17,25) and [46,52).

R 4.3.3 `gram.y`, `SpecialValue`: the lexer returns `ERROR` when a line break arrives before the second `%`, so an unterminated operator is reported where it is rather than swallowing the lines below it. Ground truth: the file is refused with `unexpected input` at the `2`.

`?Quotes` and R 4.3.3 `gram.y`: the `r` opens a raw string only where it begins a token, so a name in front of it leaves an ordinary string that closes at the second quote — and the quote after that opens one that never closes. Ground truth: R refuses the file with `unexpected string constant` at column 8, the `"`, and echoes the line cut at `z <- xr"(a "`, which is the ordinary string its lexer read there.

A quoted string carries a line break as content, so one that never closes runs to the end of the file and the transformation writes nothing. Ground truth, R 4.3.3: refused with `unexpected INCOMPLETE_STRING`.
